clusters.label: NOC_TIMEOUT
clusters.representative_signature: NOC_TIMEOUT | NOC: Transaction timeout ; NOC: NoC error register snapshot ; SYSTEM: Interconnect failure ; NOC: Fabric <*> ; NOC: DMA burst overflow

hypotheses.root_cause: Likely (weakly supported): a DMA burst overflow on channel 2 (burst_len=256) during heavy fabric congestion overran NoC buffering. A PCIE->DDR transaction (txn 0xB691) was left unserviced and timed out with -ETIME. Classic deadlock and QoS starvation are not supported by the logs.
hypotheses.rationale: Causal chain: DMA ch2 burst overflow (burst_len=256 @2.882s) during CPU<->DDR/CPU<->PCIE congestion (stall up to 31%) -> NoC buffer/tracking overrun leaves PCIE->DDR txn 0xB691 unserviced -> NOC transaction timeout rc=-62 @3.444s -> SYSTEM FATAL Interconnect failure @3.546s. The specialists agree on what is ruled out. DDR was alive with normal latency (72–84 ns) and no UE on both sides of the timeout. PMU shows no droop, gating or DVFS. PCIe has a stable Gen3 x16 link, AER=0, and a steady retrain rate. So the fault is inside the NoC. Within the NoC, the deadlock marker ('Dependency cycle suspected', as in run 000021) is missing, and the fabric kept draining after the timeout (stall 13%, then 3%), which argues against a circular deadlock. The starvation markers (QoS credit starvation / credits=0, as in run 000003) are also missing. The only catalogue marker present is one DMA burst overflow, 560 ms before the timeout and after congestion had already eased. The temporal link is therefore weak. The undecodable NOC0 register dump is the main gap, and no single question to one specialist can fill it, because it needs a register map. Confidence is kept low because this is mainly elimination plus one isolated marker. The historian's high-similarity matches (deadlock/starvation) do not fit the observed markers. (1 of 4 specialists pointed at this cause.)
recommended_actions: Decode the NOC0 REG_DUMP (0x60000BDC–0x60000C28) against the fabric register map: outstanding-txn counters, per-port credits, overflow/sticky error bits, and the txn tracker entry for 0xB691.
Repro with DMA channel 2 burst_len capped (e.g. 64/128) under the same CPU<->DDR/CPU<->PCIE congestion profile; if timeouts disappear, DMA burst overflow is confirmed.
Repro with burst_len=256 forced on ch2 under congestion to see if it reliably produces PCIE->DDR timeouts.
Enable NoC trace/transaction tracker logging for PCIE->DDR path between the overflow event and timeout to see where 0xB691 was held.
Add NoC logging of QoS credit levels and dependency-cycle checks at higher verbosity to firmly exclude starvation/deadlock.

trace.output: NOC: Decode the NOC0 error register snapshot at 3.516s for txn 0xB691 (PCIE->DDR, rc=-62). Does it point to a deadlock (circular credit/buffer dependency, stuck arbiters) like run 000021, or QoS starvation of the PCIE initiator like run 000003? Check outstanding-transaction counts, credit levels, and QoS/priority settings just before 3.444s.; DDR: Was the DDR target able to accept and complete transactions around 3.3-3.5s? Look for controller stalls, refresh/retraining, self-refresh entry, frequency changes, ECC events, or queue backpressure that could have held up the PCIE->DDR transaction 0xB691 until it timed out.; PCIE: What was the PCIE initiator doing just before the 3.444s timeout? Look for DMA bursts, a flood of outstanding requests, link state changes (L0s/L1/recovery), or error conditions that could have caused fabric congestion or left txn 0xB691 orphaned.; PMU: Were there any power-domain, clock-gating, DVFS, or voltage events affecting the NOC, DDR, or PCIE domains between ~3.3s and 3.546s (e.g., a domain gated or clock switched while transactions were still in flight) that could have caused the interconnect timeout?
trace.note: The failure is a NoC timeout on a PCIE->DDR transaction, so NOC is the main subsystem to look at. Its register dump should tell us whether this is a deadlock or QoS starvation, the two closest past incidents (sim 0.90 and 0.87). DDR is the target, so a stall there could have caused the timeout. PCIE is the initiator, so a traffic burst or link problem could have flooded the fabric. PMU is a common upstream cause, since a power or clock change during in-flight traffic can stall the interconnect. I left out BOOT, FW and THERMAL because the past incidents that involve them have low similarity. Thermal can be added if PMU shows throttling.
